title: AVWAP Reclaim
teaches: The AVWAP reclaim as we trade it: a stock above its 200-day falls hard from a high everyone can see, closes under the anchored VWAP from that high for weeks until the line flattens, then closes clearly back over it; we buy only after price proves the reclaim, never at the touch, the stop sits a few cents under the reclaim day's low, the first sell is a judgment, usually day 3 or later into a 3, 5 or 7 day push, with the rest on the trail, and a loss taken at the stop is the system working.

facts.quote: When a stock is above an advancing AVWAP, buyers are in control for that timeframe, as the average price is increasing.

facts.claim: Shannon: don't buy the dip, buy strength after.

facts.claim: D42: never own more than 1% of a stock's average daily volume.

facts.claim: Later sells are a judgment: sell more into strength on a later push, and trail what is left.

walkthroughs.title: EPC, December 2006: the flat line
steps: EPC, late 2006. It falls 18.7% off its October high and closes 42 times under the AVWAP anchored there.
Still above the 200-day. The line goes flat for a month at 52. Then one clean close over it.
Next day it trades over that day's high. Buy at market, 52.67. Stop a few cents under its low, 51.99.
A 1.3% stop. Back under the line, you're out small. Instead it ran, 3R in six sessions.

questions.q: You anchor a VWAP to the high a stock fell from. What is that line actually showing you?
choices: Buyers' average cost since the high
The highest price it's traded since then
The open of the high day
questions.answer: Buyers' average cost since the high
questions.why: Buyers' average cost since the high. Every share traded since that day goes into it, and the busy days count more. So the line shows you where the average person who bought since the top is sitting. Price under it, they're losing. Price back over it, they're winning again. And it moves every day, so it's not a flat level you draw once.
questions.lesson_line: Name the event first. The line is what everyone since then paid.

wrong.The 50-day average close: That's the 50-day moving average. No anchor, and no weighting by volume.
wrong.The highest price it's traded since then: That's a level, not an average. The AVWAP averages what people actually paid.
wrong.The open of the high day: That's just where the count starts. The line moves every day after it.

questions.simple: It's the average price buyers paid since the high, with busy days counting more.

reasons: rests on a proposed card line, av.daily_bars (+2)

questions.q: A stock closes back over the AVWAP from its old high. The average buyer since that high is back in the green.
questions.why: True. That's exactly how Shannon reads it. The AVWAP from a prior high tells you whether the average buyer since that high is winning or losing. Back over the line, they're winning again. That's when he gets interested, and so do I. It's where you start looking for proof though. It's not a buy signal on its own.
questions.lesson_line: Under the line, the average buyer since the high is losing. Back over it, they're winning.
questions.simple: True. Back over the line, the average buyer since the high is making money again.

questions.why: True. Under the 200-day we don't buy stocks. That's a hard line, and no single stock gets an exception. A big fall can drag a name under its 200-day. A reclaim of the AVWAP down there can still look great. Doesn't matter. Check the close on the reclaim day. Under the 200-day, it's a pass.
questions.lesson_line: Under the 200-day there's no long to take, however clean the line looks.
questions.simple: True. We don't buy stocks under the 200-day, so the reclaim day has to close above it.

questions.q: You're long a reclaim and it closes back under the AVWAP. That close alone is your signal to sell.
questions.why: False. The stop is your exit, not the line. Your stop already sits a few cents under the reclaim day's low, and that low is normally at or under the line. So if the reclaim really fails, the stop takes you out. A close under the line with the stop still holding is noise you planned for. Sell on every one and you get shaken out of trades that were fine.
questions.lesson_line: A close under the line isn't the exit. The stop is.
questions.simple: False. The stop is the exit, so a close under the line doesn't sell it by itself.

deeper.trap: The trap runs both ways. Some traders sell on the first close back under the line. Others drop the stop to give it room. Neither. Shannon says not to hold and hope when the line breaks. We agree in spirit. The stop under the reclaim day's low makes that call.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (A4)

questions.q: You're anchoring a VWAP the way Shannon does. Which of these dates would he pick?
choices: The major high the fall began at
The day you bought the stock
The bar with the most volume
The first trading day of the year
questions.answer: The major high the fall began at
questions.why: The major high the fall began at. Shannon anchors to dates where price really turned: major highs and lows, big news, strong reversals. His test is any date from which price movement began or reversed. That's why we anchor to the high. Everyone saw that top, and everyone who bought since is in the line. Whatever you pick, name it on the chart. A line from a high and a line from a low tell different stories.
questions.lesson_line: Anchor to an event the whole market saw. A date that makes the line fit isn't one.

wrong.The day you bought the stock: That's your event, not the market's. Nobody else cares what you paid.
wrong.The bar with the most volume: Volume alone isn't his test. He wants the date price began or reversed.
wrong.The first trading day of the year: A calendar date isn't a market event. Nothing turned there.

questions.simple: The major high, because the line should start where price really turned.

reasons: rests on held decision D-082 (which anchors count)

questions.q: On an AVWAP reclaim, your stop goes a few cents under the reclaim day's low, not right on it.
questions.why: True. The low of the day, the LOD, is where the chart says you're wrong. On this setup that's the reclaim day's low. I put the stop a few cents under it, not on it. A quick tag of the low shouldn't take me out. That low normally sits at or under the AVWAP. So if the stop hits, the reclaim has failed too, and you're out for the right reason. Stop first, then the size comes from it.
questions.lesson_line: Stop first: a few cents under the reclaim day's low.
questions.simple: True. Just under the reclaim day's low, so if it hits, the reclaim has failed too.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (A3, F62) and held decision D-008

questions.q: It's been under its AVWAP from the high for weeks. Today it closes back over. What kind of close do you want?
choices: Over by anything, even a cent
As far over the line as it can run
questions.why: Clearly over, not stretched. A close a cent over the line hasn't proved anything. It's still in the noise around the line. A close miles above it is trouble too. Your stop goes under the reclaim day's low, and that low sits at or under the line. So the further it closes above the line, the wider your stop and the fewer shares you get. I want a real close over the line that I can still risk tightly against. Judge it by eye.
questions.lesson_line: Over the line by a real margin, not a poke and not a sprint.

wrong.Over by anything, even a cent: A cent over is still sitting on the line. Nothing's proven yet.
wrong.As far over the line as it can run: A big run over the line puts your stop far away. Fewer shares, worse trade.
wrong.Sitting right on the line: On the line isn't back over it. Nothing's been taken back yet.

questions.simple: A real close over the line that still lets you keep the stop tight.

reasons: the key rests on one card line, c04 (+3)
rests on a proposed card line, av.reclaim_day_close (+2)

questions.q: Two reclaim days clear the line by the same amount. One closes at its high, one mid-range. They're equally strong.
questions.why: False. The one that closes at its high is the stronger day. Buyers held it up there right into the bell. A mid-range close means sellers leaned on it late in the day. Both can still be traded. The close at the high just grades higher, and a higher grade gets more size. Grading's a judgment, not a checklist, but this is one of the things I look at.
questions.lesson_line: Where the reclaim day closes in its range tells you who won the day.
questions.simple: False. A close at the high shows buyers held it into the bell, so it grades higher.

reasons: cites only one fact

questions.q: Shannon reads a gap up over a cluster of AVWAPs as buyers back in control.
questions.why: True. Those are his words. The gap above the AVWAPs put buyers back in control, and the cluster will likely act as support on pullbacks. We don't argue with that read. We just don't call it an AVWAP reclaim. A gap over the line skips the part we're buying, the stock taking the line back from below during the day. So we judge it as a gap setup, like a Kicker, with the gap rules.
questions.lesson_line: A gap over the line is a gap trade for us. Judge it with the gap rules.
questions.simple: True. Shannon sees buyers back in control, but we trade that gap as a gap setup.

deeper.counter: Shannon and we read the same gap two ways. He sees buyers back in control and expects the cluster to act as support on pullbacks. We judge a gap over the line as a Kicker or a gap setup. The line was never taken back from below in regular hours. Know which playbook you're using before you buy.

questions.q: A reclaim only means something after a real fall from the high, not a small dip.
questions.why: True. This whole setup is about trapped buyers. A stock drops hard off a high everyone saw, and everyone who bought up there is under water. Weeks under the line wear them out. When price takes the line back, the average buyer since the high is winning again. A small dip doesn't trap anybody, so there's nothing to reclaim. Judge it on the chart: a real drop off a real high, not a wobble.
questions.lesson_line: No real fall, no trapped buyers. The reclaim needs a fall behind it.
questions.simple: True. A small dip traps nobody, so there's nothing to win back.

reasons: the key rests on one card line, c01 (+3)
rests on a proposed card line, av.real_fall (+2)

questions.q: Two reclaims both close above the 200-day. One's 200-day is rising, the other's is rolling over. Which do you want?
questions.why: The one over a rising 200-day. Both pass the 200-day test, since both close above it. But a rising 200-day means the long-term trend still points up under you. A falling one means the bigger trend is rolling over, and your reclaim is swimming against it. That's the weaker trade, and I'd grade it lower. How far above the 200-day it sits isn't the point. Which way it's pointing is.
questions.lesson_line: Above the 200-day is a must. A rising 200-day is the better version.

wrong.The one over a falling 200-day: That's the weaker case. The bigger trend is rolling over under the trade.
wrong.No difference, above is above: Above is the must. Rising is the better version on top of it.
wrong.Whichever is further above it: Distance isn't the tell. Look at which way the 200-day is pointing.

questions.simple: The rising one, because then the long-term trend is still pointing up under you.

reasons: the key rests on one card line, c07 (+3)
rests on a proposed card cue, av.ma200_rising (+2)

questions.q: A reclaim that's run more than 10% above its 9 EMA is too stretched to buy.

And a stock that stretched tends to snap back toward its average. That's why it's a skip, not a smaller buy. You're not done with the stock. Let it come back in and set up again.
questions.lesson_line: More than 10% over the 9 EMA is too stretched. Let it come back.
questions.simple: True. Past 10% over the 9 EMA it's run too far, so we skip it and wait.

Buy only if volume is heavy

The pattern's low works too, and so does a line minus a cushion, like a stop a bit under the AVWAP. What you never do is pick the stop to fit a size you already wanted. Whichever stop you use, the size comes from it.

questions.q: This stock sat under a line that starts at its March high and moves every day. Today it closes back over. What setup is it?
choices: A Remount of a moving average
A U&R of the prior swing low
A breakout over a flat level
questions.why: An AVWAP reclaim. A line that starts on one named day and moves with price and volume is an anchored VWAP. A moving average has no anchor, and a flat level doesn't move. Anchor a VWAP to the March high on your own chart and you'll find it right around $70. MAS sat under it for 70 closes, then closed back over in July 2024. That's the picture you want: weeks under, the line going flat, then a clean close back over it.
questions.lesson_line: Name the line first. An anchor day and volume make it an AVWAP.

wrong.A Remount of a moving average: A moving average has no anchor day. This line starts on the March high.
wrong.A U&R of the prior swing low: A U&R dips under a low and is back over within 3 sessions. This sat under for weeks.
wrong.A breakout over a flat level: A flat level is one price. This line moves every day.

questions.simple: An AVWAP reclaim, because the line starts on one day and moves with price and volume.

reasons: rests on held decision D-082 (which anchors count)

questions.q: The AVWAP on a daily chart gives you the exact same number as the intraday line.
questions.why: False. Built from daily bars, it's an approximation of the intraday line. Close, not exact. Shannon says to use as short a timeframe as you can for the most accurate VWAP. So don't fuss over a few cents. Read the daily line as a zone. A close that barely ticks over it hasn't proven anything anyway.
questions.lesson_line: The daily line is close, not exact. Read it as a zone.
questions.simple: False. The daily line is close to the intraday one, so read it as a zone.

questions.q: It reclaims its AVWAP from the high, but another AVWAP, from its IPO high, sits 3% overhead. How does that change your read?
choices: Grades it down, a ceiling is close
Grades it up, two lines agree
No change, only the reclaim counts
No trade with a line above it

With that line only 3% above you, the stock runs into that selling almost right away. It's still a trade. It's just not my best one, and I'd size it like a lower grade. Clear air up to the next line is what I want.
questions.lesson_line: Look up before you buy. The next line is where it meets sellers.

wrong.No trade with a line above it: It's a grade call, not a deal breaker. Still a trade, just a smaller one.

wrong.No change, only the reclaim counts: Always look up. The next line overhead is where the selling waits.

questions.q: We take no new reclaim buy in the 3 sessions before an earnings report.
questions.why: True. Three days out from a report, I don't open anything new. The report can gap the stock right through your stop, and a stop can't catch a gap. If you're already in, you can hold through it only if you're up 5R. The earnings-AVWAP version of this setup forms after the report anyway, so it rarely runs into one. Check the calendar before you even look at the chart.
questions.lesson_line: Check the calendar before the chart.
questions.simple: True. A report can gap it through your stop, so no new buys in the 3 days before one.

questions.q: Months above a rising AVWAP, a two-day dip under it, then a close back over. Is that the reclaim you buy?
questions.story: The stock held above the rising AVWAP from its March high for months. Tuesday it dips under the line. Thursday it closes back over.
choices: No, it barely spent time under
No, it must close an ATR over
Yes, a rising line adds strength
questions.answer: No, it barely spent time under
questions.why: No. That's a dip, not a reclaim. The setup we buy comes after weeks of closes under the line. That's long enough for the people who bought up high to get worn out, and for the line to flatten. Here the stock held above a rising line for months and slipped under it for a couple of days. Nobody got trapped. Shannon says to watch the line's direction more than a close or two either side, and this line never stopped rising.
questions.lesson_line: Count the closes under the line. A few days is a dip. Weeks under a flat line is a reclaim.

wrong.Yes, it closed back over: A close back over isn't enough. It needs weeks under a line that's gone flat first.
wrong.No, it must close an ATR over: No set distance is the issue. The miss is that it barely spent time under the line.
wrong.Yes, a rising line adds strength: A rising line it barely dipped under is a different trade. Nothing was reclaimed.

questions.simple: No. A couple of days under a rising line is a dip, not weeks under a flat one.

deeper.counter: A quick dip under a rising line that closes back over can look like a fresh reclaim. The setup we want is the opposite picture. Weeks of closes under the line, the line gone flat, then the first close back over. Shannon reads the line's direction first, and this one kept rising the whole time.

questions.q: It's closed under its AVWAP from the high for weeks. This morning it rallies right up into the line. Do you buy the touch?
questions.story: Weeks of closes under the AVWAP from the high. Today it trades up and tags the line from below.
choices: No, wait till it proves it
Yes, with a stop under the line
No, only buy it on a pullback

Shannon calls the line a level of interest, not a place to do business: don't buy the dip, buy strength after. So I wait for a clear close back over, then buy as it trades through the reclaim day's high.

wrong.Yes, with a stop under the line: A stop doesn't turn a touch into a buy. You'd just be buying into the sellers.
wrong.No, only buy it on a pullback: Right call, wrong reason. You're waiting for strength back over the line, not a dip.

choices: Buy it with a wider stop
questions.why: Pass. 52.40 minus 50.00 is 2.40, and 2.40 over 50.00 is 4.8%. We never buy more than 4% over the trigger. Here's why it matters. Your stop doesn't move up with the price. It stays under the reclaim day's low. So the further you chase, the wider your stop and the fewer shares you can buy. You'd be paying more for a worse trade. I'd rather miss it than chase it.
questions.lesson_line: I'd rather miss it than chase it.

wrong.Buy, 4.8% is close enough: 4% is the line, and 4.8% is past it. Close enough is how chasing starts.
wrong.Pass, the reclaim already failed: Nothing's failed. It's trading above the trigger. The problem is distance.
wrong.Buy it with a wider stop: A wider stop means fewer shares for the same risk. That's the cost of chasing, not a fix.

questions.simple: Pass. It's 4.8% over the trigger and we never chase more than 4%.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook, C28 (+2)
the key is arithmetic on the story's numbers (+2)

questions.q: It gapped right through your stop this morning. Where's your stop now?
questions.story: You bought at 50.00 with the stop at 49.00. It gaps open at 48.70, under your stop. The first 30-minute bar runs from 48.40 to 49.30.
choices: Sell it all at the open
Out now, the loss is past 2R
questions.why: 48.40. A gap through your stop is the one time the stop moves. You don't panic-sell the open. You let the first 30 minutes play out, and the low of that first 30-minute bar is your new stop. There's a ceiling. If those 30 minutes take the loss past 2R, you're out. Your R here is a dollar, 50.00 to 49.00. 48.40 is less than two dollars under the fill, so you're inside 2R.
questions.lesson_line: A gap through the stop is the one exception. The first 30 minutes decide.

wrong.49.30, the first 30-minute high: It's the low of that first bar, not the high.
wrong.Sell it all at the open: The open isn't the exit on a gap. The first 30 minutes decide.
wrong.Out now, the loss is past 2R: Your R is a dollar. 48.40 is less than two dollars under 50.00, so it's inside 2R.

questions.simple: 48.40. When it gaps through your stop, the low of the first 30 minutes is the new stop.

deeper.trap: The ceiling matters. Had that first 30-minute low sat more than two dollars under the 50.00 fill, the loss would be past 2R. Then you just get out. You don't wait around for a new low to form.

reasons: computed key
rests on the owner's rulebook (B20)

questions.q: A reclaim you missed has run for days. The 9 EMA is 40.00 and it trades 44.80. How stretched is it over the 9 EMA?
questions.why: 12.0%. 44.80 minus 40.00 is 4.80. 4.80 over 40.00 is 12.0%. That's past our 10% line, so I skip it. Not a smaller buy, a skip. From that far up your stop's a long way below, and the snap back toward the 9 EMA can come any day. If you like the stock, let it rest and come back to you.
questions.lesson_line: Measure the stretch from the 9 EMA before you buy.
questions.simple: 12.0%, past our 10% line, so it's too stretched to buy.

reasons: cites only one fact
computed key
rests on the owner's rulebook (C29)

wrong.112.0%: Compared price to the average without taking the 9 EMA off first.
wrong.48.0%: Divided the gap by 10, not by the 9 EMA.

questions.q: Next day it never reaches your alert, and it closes back under the AVWAP. What now?
questions.story: The reclaim day closed clearly over the line. Your buy alert sits just over its high.
choices: Kill the alert, the setup's off
Keep it, the trigger's still live
Buy the next close back over
Kill it, the reclaim was too small
questions.answer: Kill the alert, the setup's off
questions.why: Kill the alert. The reclaim has to hold until you buy. If it slips back under the line before the trigger trades, the buyers lost that fight, and there's no trade. Buying the next morning anyway means buying a failed reclaim. If it closes back over later, that's a brand-new reclaim, and you judge it from scratch.
questions.lesson_line: The reclaim has to hold until the buy. If it slips first, walk away.

wrong.Keep it, the trigger's still live: The close back under came before the trigger. That ends this one.
wrong.Buy the next close back over: A new close over is a new reclaim, judged from scratch. This one's off.
wrong.Kill it, the reclaim was too small: Right call, wrong reason. The reclaim day was fine. The close back under ended it.

questions.simple: The setup's off. It slipped back under the line before your buy, so you walk away.

reasons: rests on a proposed card line, av.inv_close_back_before_trigger (+2)
the conflicts line ties it to the held trigger decision, D-003 (+2)

questions.q: After the buy, an AVWAP reclaim that trades down to the stop is sold at the stop.
questions.why: True. The stop is the exit. It only moves up, never down or wider. Shannon: don't hold and hope.
questions.lesson_line: My stop is my stop. That is the whole rule.

questions.q: Four software names reclaim the same week, yours among them. How does that change the grade on yours?
questions.story: A correction just ended. Four software stocks reclaim their AVWAPs from their highs in the same week.
choices: No change, only my chart counts
Up, but only on heavy volume
questions.why: Up. When a whole group takes its lines back the same week, that's money flowing into the group, not one stock bouncing. It's best right after a correction, when the leaders are the first to get back over their AVWAPs from their highs. Your stock isn't fighting alone. It's a plus for the grade though, not a must. A lone reclaim can work too.
questions.lesson_line: One reclaim is a stock. Several in one group is a move.

wrong.Down, the trade's too crowded: Several names moving together is the group getting bought, not a crowded trade.
wrong.No change, only my chart counts: The group matters. A stock moving with its group has help.
wrong.Up, but only on heavy volume: The plus is the group moving together. Volume isn't part of it.

questions.simple: Up. A whole group reclaiming together after a correction means money is coming in.

reasons: cites only one fact
rests on a proposed card criterion (av.group_reclaims)

questions.q: Everything looked right, and you got stopped out on day 2. What did the stop just do for you?
questions.story: Bought the reclaim at 262.81, stop 255.97, after a big fall, 47 closes under and a flat AVWAP. Day 2 takes the stop. Weeks later, the low is 12.7% under your buy.
choices: Nothing, the line was the exit
questions.why: Its job. Everything going in was right: a big fall, 47 closes under the line, the line flat. Look at the last bar, though. It closed down near its low, under your fill. That's a warning, not a sell. The stop decides, and on day 2 it said the reclaim failed. 262.81 to 255.97 is a 2.6% stop, and you lost 1R. Weeks later AMZN's low was 12.7% under your buy. Holding would have cost about five times as much. Good setups fail too. That's what the stop is for.
questions.lesson_line: A loss taken at plan is the system working.

wrong.Cost you, it needed room: Room meant a 12.7% hole. The stop cost 1R, holding would've cost about five times that.
wrong.Nothing, the line was the exit: The stop is the exit, not the line. Here the stop did the work.
wrong.Proved the setup was bad: The setup was fine. Good setups fail too, and a stop is for exactly that.

questions.simple: It did its job. It kept the loss to 1R when holding would have cost about five times more.

reasons: rests on held decision D-008
fixed before (cold check)

questions.q: You got stopped out the session after you bought. Weeks later the setup triggers again. Do you take it?
questions.story: Bought the reclaim at 192.63 with the stop at 189.29. The next session takes the stop.
choices: Yes, as a new trade, new stop
Yes, but with a wider stop
No, wait a month after a stop
questions.answer: Yes, as a new trade, new stop
questions.why: Yes, as a new trade. A stop-out isn't a verdict on the stock. If the setup triggers again, it's a fresh trade with its own stop, its own size and every rule. We cap it at 3 tries in a week and 6 in a month on one name. That stops you feeding a stock that isn't working. LIN is the lesson. Stopped the next session in September 2019, it held the line for weeks and printed 3R 39 sessions later, without us.
questions.lesson_line: A stop-out isn't a verdict on the stock. The next trigger is a new trade.

wrong.Yes, but with a wider stop: A new trade gets its own stop under its own low. Nothing calls for a wider one.
wrong.No, one try per line: The cap is 3 tries a week and 6 a month, not one.
wrong.No, wait a month after a stop: No rule makes you wait. A new trigger is a new trade.

questions.simple: Yes. A new trigger is a new trade with its own stop, up to 3 tries a week.

deeper.example: LIN, September 2019. Bought at 192.63 with a stop at 189.29, it was stopped the next session. Then it held the line for weeks, and the 3R level printed 39 sessions later without us. The stop was still right. Getting back in needed a new trigger, as a new trade with its own stop.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook, B21 and E56 (+2)
two wrong choices were shortened in the first cold check (+1)

questions.q: Friday, day 5, it gaps open at 3.3R. What do you do at the open?
questions.story: Your reclaim was bought Monday and pushed up all week. It closed Thursday at 2.7R.
choices: Weigh selling some into the gap
Sell a third, the gap forces it
Sell it all at the open
questions.answer: Weigh selling some into the gap
questions.why: Weigh selling some into the gap. Day 5 of a push, gapping up, is right where a first sell often makes sense. We like selling into a 3, 5 or 7 day push. But it's a judgment, not a rule, and the gap doesn't force anything. If it's acting great, you can let it run. If it feels like the end of the push, sell some into that strength. What you don't do is dump it all, or chase the gap with more shares.
questions.lesson_line: A gap into a 5 day push is a spot to weigh the first sell. It's never a rule.

wrong.Sell a third, the gap forces it: A gap is never a rule to sell. It's your call.
wrong.Sell it all at the open: The first sell is part of it. The rest keeps working on the trail.
wrong.Add shares, it gapped up: A gap is a spot to weigh selling, not buying. Adding is rare, a feel call, never the plan.

questions.simple: Weigh selling some. Day 5 into a gap is a good spot, but the gap never forces it.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook, F63 and B19 (+2)

questions.q: A reclaim that's gone nowhere gets 20 trading days to get past 1R before you sell it.
questions.why: False. It's 10 trading days, not 20. Still under 1R after 10 days and I sell it. A trade that isn't working ties up money and attention you could put in something that is. Your price stop runs the whole time too. The time stop just cleans out the dead ones.
questions.lesson_line: Ten days and nothing. The money has somewhere better to be.
questions.simple: False. Still under 1R after 10 trading days, we sell it and move the money.

reasons: cites only one fact
rests on the owner's rulebook (C33)

questions.q: Your reclaim is working. When does your stop come up to breakeven?
choices: The next day, to be safe
As soon as it closes over the line
questions.why: Somewhere between 2R and 5R, or when you make your first sell. It's a judgment inside that window, not one fixed number. Move it the next day and normal wiggle stops you out of a trade that's working. Once it's up a few R though, there's no reason to let a good winner turn into a loss. The stop only ever moves up, so breakeven is fine.
questions.lesson_line: Breakeven comes between 2R and 5R of gain, not on day one.

wrong.The next day, to be safe: Way too soon. Normal wiggle takes you out of a good trade.
wrong.Never, the stop stays put: The stop can move up. Breakeven at 2R to 5R is fine.
wrong.As soon as it closes over the line: Every reclaim closes over the line. That's the setup, not 2R of gain.

questions.simple: Between 2R and 5R, or at your first sell, so a good winner can't turn into a loss.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (B19, A4)
key reworded in this upgrade

questions.q: Your honest stop, a few cents under today's low, is 4.1% under tomorrow's fill. Wider than you like. What do you do?
questions.story: The reclaim day. Tomorrow's trigger sits just over today's high.
choices: Keep the stop, buy fewer shares
Use the AVWAP as the stop
Same shares, the stop is honest
questions.answer: Keep the stop, buy fewer shares
questions.why: Keep the stop and buy fewer shares. The size comes from the stop, never the other way around. 4.1% is wider than I like, but up to 5% I'll take it. Pull the stop up just to fit more shares and normal noise takes you out of a good trade. Keep the shares and the stop, and you're risking more than you planned. So fewer shares. If even that doesn't fit your risk, skip it.
questions.lesson_line: You never pick a size and back-fit a stop.

wrong.Use the AVWAP as the stop: The line isn't the stop. Ours goes a few cents under the reclaim day's low.
wrong.Pull the stop up to 3%: That's tightening into the noise to fit a size. Never.
wrong.Same shares, the stop is honest: The stop's honest, but same shares on a wider stop risks more than you planned.

questions.simple: Keep the honest stop and buy fewer shares, or skip it if even that doesn't fit.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook, A3, A5 and A13 (+2)

questions.q: In our scan of AVWAP reclaims, the loudest reclaim days hit 3R more often than the quiet ones.
questions.why: False. It went the other way. Reclaim days on 1.5x the 50-day volume or more reached 3R 22.3% of the time. The quiet ones, under 1.0x, got there 27.0% of the time. So don't sit out a clean reclaim because the volume's light. Volume raises the grade when it's there. It's never a must. And that's one scan of our own data, not a promise.
questions.lesson_line: Loud volume on the reclaim day didn't pick the winners. Don't wait on it.
questions.simple: False. In our scan the quiet reclaim days actually reached 3R a bit more often.

deeper.counter: It's natural to want heavy volume on the day a stock takes back a line. Our scan of AVWAP reclaims didn't back that. Days on 1.5x the 50-day average or more reached 3R 22.3% of the time. Days under 1.0x reached it 27.0%. It's one scan of our own daily bars, a measure and not a rule.

reasons: cites only one fact
a scan statistic that can change with the data
rests on held decision D-006 (volume as a cue)

questions.q: What changes on your next AVWAP reclaim?
questions.story: Bought at 43.22, stop 42.43. The next session takes the stop. The next 10 closes are all back under the line. Its low over the next twenty sessions is 11.6% under your buy.
choices: Widen the stop on the next one
Buy the dip under the line
questions.why: Nothing. You followed every rule and the reclaim failed. The stop took you out the next session at 1R. All of the next 10 closes were back under the line. The low over the next 20 sessions was 11.6% under the buy. The stop is the exit, so the same stop goes on the next trade.
questions.lesson_line: You will take this loss again. It is the price of the ones that run.

wrong.Buy the dip under the line: That adds to a failed reclaim. The stop is the exit, and it never moves down.
wrong.Widen the stop on the next one: A wider stop here would have ridden it down 11.6%. The stop worked.
wrong.Stop trading AVWAP reclaims: One planned loss is not a verdict on the setup. In our examples the stop kept each failure to 1R.

questions.simple: Nothing, because you followed the plan and the stop kept a small loss from becoming a much bigger one.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (A4)
fixed before (cold check)

questions.q: Today it closes back over its AVWAP from a September high. The line's still sloping down. Do you take it?
questions.story: The reclaim day. It closes back over the AVWAP from a September high. Over the 10 sessions before, that line fell 0.56 ATR.
choices: Yes, it closed over the line
Yes, a steep line breaks harder
No, it needs a close 1 ATR over
questions.why: No. That line's still falling right into the reclaim. Shannon's take: a move above a declining VWAP will often fail, and the steeper the angle, the likelier it fails. A falling line means the selling since the high hasn't let up. I want the line to go flat first, so the sellers are worn out before I buy. AAPL ran anyway this time. That's fine. You pass on the weaker picture, and some weaker pictures still work.
questions.lesson_line: A move above a falling line often fails. Wait for it to flatten.

wrong.Yes, it closed over the line: The close is one piece. The line still sloping down is the problem.
wrong.Yes, a steep line breaks harder: The reverse. The steeper the line, the likelier a move over it fails.
wrong.No, it needs a close 1 ATR over: Right call, wrong reason. The miss is the falling line, not the size of the close.

questions.simple: No. The line's still falling, and a move over a falling line often fails.

deeper.trap: AAPL in October: its line was still falling into the reclaim, and it ran to 9.3R anyway. That doesn't make waiting for a flat line wrong. It's a quality filter, not a prediction. It keeps you out of the weaker case, and some weaker cases still win.

reasons: rests on a proposed card line, av.line_flattened, whose 0.5 ATR is the dossier's number (+2)

questions.q: It slipped off a one-month high, closed under that AVWAP 19 times, and today closes back over. Would you take this reclaim?
questions.story: The reclaim day. It sat under the AVWAP from a one-month high for 19 closes. Today it closes back over.
choices: No, that's a dip, not a real fall
Yes, 19 closes under is enough here
questions.answer: No, that's a dip, not a real fall
questions.why: No. The candle's fine, a hammer that closed right at its high. The problem is the high behind it. A one-month high isn't the kind of high the whole market remembers. The pullback off it was a dip, not a real fall. Not enough people got trapped up there. We want a big high everyone saw and a real drop off it. Then a reclaim means those buyers are finally winning again. ADC did run after this one. Fine. Passing on a so-so picture that works isn't a mistake.
questions.lesson_line: Anchor to a high that mattered, and a fall that trapped people.

wrong.Yes, it closed back over: The close over is the last step. The fall behind it has to be real first.
wrong.Yes, 19 closes under is enough here: Time under is one piece. The high and the fall have to matter too.
wrong.No, it must fall 10% first: There's no percent line. Judge the fall by eye: a real drop off a big high.

questions.simple: No. A small pullback off a one-month high traps nobody, so there's nothing to reclaim.

deeper.trap: ADC: a shallow dip off a one-month high, reclaimed after 19 closes under. It ran to 6.4R anyway. A winner you passed on isn't a mistake. Passing on weaker pictures will miss some winners, and that's the trade-off.

reasons: rests on a proposed card line, av.real_fall (+2)

questions.q: After weeks under a flat AVWAP, it closes just barely over the line. What's that telling you?
questions.story: The reclaim day. The close sits 0.23 ATR over the line.
choices: A poke in the noise, pass
A U&R of the line, go long
questions.answer: A poke in the noise, pass
questions.why: A poke, so pass. 0.23 ATR is a hair over the line. On a daily chart, where the line itself is only close to exact, that's still inside the noise. Nothing's proven yet. CAG did this, filled the trigger the next day and chopped around to 2.7R before a December gap did the real work. I want a close that clearly clears the line.
questions.lesson_line: A hair over the line is still the line. Clear it.

wrong.A clean reclaim, go long: Clean means clearly over the line. This is barely over it.
wrong.A U&R of the line, go long: A U&R is back over within a few days. This sat under for weeks.
wrong.Stretched, wait for a dip: The opposite. It's barely over the line, not too far over it.

questions.simple: Pass. It's barely over the line, still in the noise, so nothing is proven yet.

reasons: rests on a proposed card line, av.reclaim_day_close (+2)

questions.q: After weeks under its AVWAP, it gaps up and opens well above the line. What setup are you looking at?
questions.story: The reclaim day. It opens 0.91 ATR above the line and closes over it.
choices: A gap setup, not a reclaim
questions.answer: A gap setup, not a reclaim
questions.why: A gap setup. The reclaim we buy is the stock taking the line back from below, during the day, through the sellers sitting there. This one opened 0.91 ATR over the line, so it skipped that whole fight overnight. We judge that as a gap trade, like a Kicker, with the gap rules. Shannon reads a gap like this as buyers back in control, and he's right. It's just a different playbook. AGCO ran to 3.1R, as a gap.
questions.lesson_line: Look at the open. A gap over the line is judged as a gap.

wrong.A clean reclaim from below: A reclaim takes the line back from below during the day. This one gapped over it.
wrong.A U&R of the AVWAP: A U&R dips under a level and comes back. This gapped over a line it was under.
wrong.A Remount of the AVWAP: A Remount takes back a moving average or a flat level. This gapped over an AVWAP.

questions.simple: A gap setup. It opened well above the line instead of taking it back from below.

deeper.counter: Shannon reads it differently. He wrote that a gap above a cluster of AVWAPs put buyers back in control. We keep our own split: a gap over the line is judged as a gap setup. AGCO opened 0.91 ATR over its line and reached 3.1R, judged as a gap, not as an AVWAP reclaim.

reasons: rests on a proposed card line, av.no_gap_over, where Shannon reads it differently (+2)
a wrong choice was shortened in the first cold check (+1)

questions.q: The stock trades 3,000,000 shares a day on average. What's the most you'd ever own?
choices: No ceiling if the stop is tight
questions.why: 30,000 shares. We never own more than 1% of a stock's average daily volume, and 1% of 3,000,000 is 30,000. The reason is getting out. Own a big chunk of a day's trading and when you sell, you're the one pushing the price down on yourself. It's a ceiling, not a target. Your risk math sets the size, and this just caps it.
questions.lesson_line: One percent of the daily volume, and not a share more.

wrong.No ceiling if the stop is tight: The volume cap is its own rule. A tight stop doesn't make a big position easy to sell.
wrong.300,000 shares, 10% of daily volume: That's 10% of the day's volume. Our ceiling is 1%.
wrong.3,000 shares, 0.1% of daily volume: That's 0.1%, way under the ceiling. The cap is 1%, which is 30,000 shares.

questions.simple: 30,000 shares, because we never own more than 1% of the daily volume.

reasons: computed key
rests on the owner's rulebook (D42)

questions.q: A reclaim is a better bet when QQQ or SPY sits above its own AVWAP from its last major low.
questions.why: True. You want the market at your back. Say the index is over its AVWAP from its last big low. Then the average buyer since that low is winning. That's a market that backs breakouts. TMO shows the other side: a clean-looking reclaim in a year the market fell, and it never got going before the stop. It's a plus I look for, not a must. Grading stays a judgment.
questions.lesson_line: Check the index's own line too. You want the market at your back.
questions.simple: True. When the index is over its own line, the market's buyers are winning too.

reasons: cites only one fact
rests on a proposed card criterion (av.index_above_avwap)

questions.q: It's an $8 stock trading about $5 million a day. Can you take it?
questions.story: The chart's textbook: weeks under a flat AVWAP, then a clean close back over it.
choices: Yes, at half size to be safe
No, only the dollar volume fails
questions.why: No. We only trade stocks at $10 or more that do at least $20 million a day. This one misses both: $8 a share and about $5 million a day. Thin names gap and slip on you, and you can't get out clean when you need to. Even the line gets less reliable, since thin trading can distort the AVWAP. I'd never trade it, however clean it looks.
questions.lesson_line: A clean line in a thin stock is still a thin stock.

wrong.Yes, the reclaim is clean: The chart's fine, the stock isn't ours. Liquidity comes before the chart.
wrong.Yes, at half size to be safe: Size doesn't make a thin stock liquid. It's off the list.
wrong.No, only the dollar volume fails: Right call, half the reason. The $8 price fails too. The floor is $10.

questions.simple: No. We only trade stocks over $10 that do at least $20 million a day.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook, B23 (+2)
two wrong choices were shortened in the first cold check (+1)

questions.q: It held the gap day's low and never closed under the earnings AVWAP. Which setup are you looking at?
questions.story: After an earnings gap up, a stock drifts back for a few days. It turns up just above the gap day's low.
choices: A Remount of a moving average
A U&R of the gap day's low
questions.why: Gap Support. First ask which side of the line the stock is on. This one held the gap day's low from above and never went under the earnings AVWAP. That's Gap Support: you buy the test that holds. The earnings-AVWAP reclaim is the other side. It buys the first close back over the line from below, after weeks stuck under it. Same line, opposite trades.
questions.lesson_line: Holding above the line is Gap Support. Back over it from below is the reclaim.

wrong.A reclaim after weeks under: A reclaim comes from below after weeks under the line. This never went under.
wrong.A U&R of the gap day's low: A U&R dips under a prior low and closes back above it. This one held the low and never dipped under.
wrong.A Remount of a moving average: A Remount takes back a moving average or a flat level. Here the stock held the gap day's low from above.

questions.simple: Gap Support. It held above the gap day's low and never went under the line.

deeper.trap: The trap is calling any bounce near an earnings gap a reclaim. Ask which side of the line the stock is on. Gap Support buys a test that holds the gap-up day's low from above. The earnings AVWAP reclaim buys the first close back over the line from below, after weeks under it.

reasons: rests on held decision D-082 (earnings anchors)

questions.q: The typical price behind our AVWAP is the average of the day's open, high and low.
questions.why: False. Typical price is the average of the day's high, low and close. The open is not in it. ChartSchool's formula: (H+L+C)/3. Our card builds the AVWAP from it: typical price times volume, summed from the anchor day, divided by the summed volume.
questions.lesson_line: High, low and close, averaged, weighted by volume, summed from the anchor.
questions.simple: False, typical price uses the high, low and close, not the open.

reasons: stable: ChartSchool's formula, re-checked 2026-11-12, and the card agree

questions.q: Brian Shannon calls a breakout above the AVWAP a mechanical signal to buy.
questions.why: False. Shannon says the opposite. To him the AVWAP is a place to look for evidence, not a mechanical signal. Some charting tools do sell a cross over the line as a buy signal. We side with Shannon. The line tells you where to look. The proof is a clear close back over a line that's gone flat, then the trigger.
questions.lesson_line: The line is where to look for evidence, not what to do.
questions.simple: False. Shannon says the line is where you look for proof, not a signal to buy.

deeper.counter: TrendSpider's help page: a trader may look for a breakout above the Anchored VWAP as a signal to enter a long position. Shannon calls the AVWAP a place to look for evidence, not a mechanical signal. On this point we side with Shannon. A cross shows where to look. A clear close back over a flattened line is the evidence.

reasons: reworded by the first cold check (+1); both quotes re-checked 2026-11-12

questions.q: It's been back and forth across the line all month. Today it closes clearly over. Take it?
questions.story: In the last month it closed over its AVWAP, back under, over again and under again. Today it closes well clear of the line.
choices: Pass, it's chopping on the line
Buy, the line is well tested
Pass, a real reclaim gaps over it
questions.answer: Pass, it's chopping on the line
questions.why: Pass. That's chop. It's crossed the line four times in a month, so nobody's in control. Shannon calls that indecision: price swinging above and below the AVWAP. One more clear close doesn't undo it. The reclaim I want is the first clean close back over after weeks under, with no back and forth. Here the sellers at even keep getting fresh chances to get out.
questions.lesson_line: Many crossings mean nobody's in control. Wait for the first clean one.

wrong.Buy, it closed clearly over: Clearly over, for the third time this month. That's a poke in a chop.
wrong.Buy, the line is well tested: Back and forth is indecision, not a tested level.
wrong.Pass, a real reclaim gaps over it: The reverse. A gap over the line is a gap setup. The reason to pass is the chop.

questions.simple: Pass. It keeps flipping across the line, which is chop, not a first clean reclaim.

deeper.trap: The trap is the word clearly. The close alone looks fine. The pass comes from the history: the line's been crossed back and forth, which Shannon reads as indecision. Look at the month before the reclaim before you judge the close.

questions.q: What did the scan not see?
questions.story: A 9.6 ATR fall, then a reclaim close 0.78 ATR over the line on 1.54x volume. It is stopped with 0.0R. The broad market fell that year.
questions.why: The market. A clean-looking reclaim in a year the broad market fell, stopped with 0.0R. The index's own standing matters.
questions.lesson_line: Read the market before the line.

questions.q: You've made your sells into strength. Now the market breaks and the stock slides. What protects the rest?
questions.story: Bought on the reclaim. It pushed to 5R and you sold some into the strength. Then the market breaks hard and the stock starts to slide.
choices: The original stop under the low
A close back under the AVWAP
questions.why: The trail. What's left rides the 9 EMA on a fast mover, or the 20 EMA on a steadier one. You sell on a close below it. Your original stop is way down there by now, and giving all that back isn't the plan. The trail keeps you in while the trend holds and gets you out when it breaks. O in January 2020 shows why. It hit 5R, then fell by half.
questions.lesson_line: Sell some into strength. The trail decides the rest.

wrong.The original stop under the low: Your stop can move up. The plan for the rest is the trail, not the starting stop.
wrong.A close back under the AVWAP: A close under the line isn't an exit after the buy. The trail decides what's left.
wrong.The 50-day, sold on a touch: We trail the 9 or 20 EMA, and we sell on a close below, not a touch.

questions.simple: The 9 or 20 EMA trail. You sell what's left on a close below that average.

deeper.example: O, January 2020: it reached 5R, then fell by half. Whatever you sold on the way up is banked. Only what's left still rides, and a close below the trailing average ends it.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (B19, E51, E52)

questions.q: You bought at 52.67 with the stop at 51.99. You sell part at 56.07. How many R did that sale bank?
questions.why: 5.0R. Your R is 52.67 minus 51.99, which is 0.68 a share. The gain is 56.07 minus 52.67, which is 3.40. 3.40 over 0.68 is 5.0R. That's a nice spot for a first sell, right in the 5 to 10R zone where we often like to sell some. When and how much is still your call. EPC hit 3R in six sessions and ran to 18.9R.
questions.lesson_line: Count every sale in R. This one banked 5R.
questions.simple: 5.0R. The 3.40 gain divided by 0.68 of risk a share.

deeper.trap: A common slip divides the gain by the fill price. That gives a percent gain, not an R count. Count sales in R: the gain divided by the fill minus the stop.

questions.q: The flat AVWAP from the high and the 50-day sit right on top of each other. How does that grade the reclaim?
questions.story: The reclaim day, after a 19.2% fall. The AVWAP from the high is flat near 70, and the 50-day sits within one ATR of it. It closes 0.49 ATR over the line.
choices: Up, the line sits at a second level
Down, too many lines in one place
questions.answer: Up, the line sits at a second level
questions.why: Up. Two levels in one spot make a stronger floor. Shannon says a level is more likely to matter with confluence. Here the flat line near 70 and the 50-day sit together, so buyers are defending one zone, not two. MAS, bought at 71.15 with the stop at 69.53, hit 3R in eight sessions. It's a plus for the grade though. Still a judgment, not a score.
questions.lesson_line: One line is a level. Two lines in one place is a shelf.

wrong.Down, too many lines in one place: Lines stacked in one place is support, not a mess. It grades up.
wrong.No change, the 50-day doesn't count: The 50-day at the line is exactly the second level you want.
wrong.Down, the 50-day sits overhead: It's at the line, not overhead. A level at the line grades up.

questions.simple: Up. The line and the 50-day sit in one spot, and two levels together hold better.

deeper.example: MAS, July 2024: after a 19.2% fall, a long flat line near 70. On 2024-07-12 it closed 0.49 ATR over the line, with the 50-day within one ATR. Bought at 71.15 with a stop at 69.53, it reached 3R in eight sessions.

questions.q: A clean reclaim triggers tomorrow. The earnings reaction day comes two sessions after that. Do you buy?
questions.story: The day before the trigger. The chart is as clean as they come.
choices: Yes, at half size for the report
No, it has to be up 5R first
questions.why: No. We don't open anything new in the 3 days before a report, and this buy lands two sessions before the reaction day. A report can gap a stock straight through your stop, and no stop catches that. The 5R part of the rule is for holding a trade you already own through a report. It's not a pass for new buys. CDW did exactly this and ran 22.4R. Still a pass. Next time it's a gap down.
questions.lesson_line: A winner the rules forbid is still a pass. Next time it's a gap down.

wrong.Yes, the reclaim is clean: Clean is the chart. The calendar still says no.
wrong.No, it has to be up 5R first: Right call, mixed-up rule. 5R is for holding an open trade through a report, not a new buy.
wrong.Yes, at half size for the report: Half size doesn't fix a gap through your stop. No new buy this close to a report.

questions.simple: No. The report is two sessions away, and we don't buy in the 3 days before one.

deeper.trap: CDW, February 2019: a clean reclaim that ran 22.4R. The buy came two sessions before its earnings reaction day, so we pass. A winner the rule keeps you out of still teaches the rule. The next report could just as easily gap down through your stop.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook, B22 (+2)

questions.q: In our scan, reclaims with stops wider than 3% reached 3R more often than tighter ones.
questions.why: False. The wide ones did worst. Stops over 3% reached 3R 22.5% of the time. Stops of 2% to 3% got there 29.3% of the time, and 2% or less 26.5%. Part of that is just math, since a wider stop puts 3R further away. Either way it fits how I trade. I almost never take a loss greater than 3%.
questions.lesson_line: A tight, honest stop is part of the edge, not just the risk.
questions.simple: False. In our scan the reclaims with stops over 3% reached 3R least often.

deeper.trap: Don't read this as proof that tight stops win. A 3R target sits three times the stop away, so a wider stop also puts 3R further off. The scan measured what happened, not why. Either way it fits how we trade: the stop usually sits within about 3% of the buy.

questions.q: Do you take the B?
questions.story: Our market filter reads Orange, one step from Red: the market's under pressure. A reclaim triggers this morning, and you grade it a B.
choices: No, Orange is A+ setups only
Yes, full size as in Green
Yes, Orange just means half size
questions.answer: No, Orange is A+ setups only
questions.why: No. In Orange I only take my best ideas, the A+ setups. The market's under pressure, and breakouts fail more when it isn't backing them. So I want the cleanest setup with the tightest risk, nothing less. A B can wait for a better market. Orange isn't a size setting. It narrows what you take. Yellow is smaller and fewer, Green is full risk, Red is mostly cash.
questions.lesson_line: Orange narrows you to the best. A B reclaim waits.

wrong.Yes, full size as in Green: Full risk is Green. Orange takes only A+ setups.
wrong.Yes, Orange just means half size: Orange is about which setups, not size. A B waits.
wrong.No, Orange means no longs: Right call, wrong reading. Red is mostly cash. Orange still takes the A+.

questions.simple: No. In Orange we only take A+ setups, and this one's a B.

deeper.trap: The trap is reading Orange as half size. Orange narrows which setups you take. Yellow is the reading for smaller and fewer. A B setup waits for a better market or a better setup.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook, F65 (+2)

questions.q: You've got an A+ reclaim, our cleanest grade, in a Green market. How much of the account do you risk?
questions.why: 1% to 1.5%. A+ is the cleanest setup we grade, so it gets our biggest risk. A and B get 0.5% to 1%, and B- or lower 0.25% to 0.5%. Green means full risk for the grade. Then the stop turns that risk into shares. It doesn't pick the risk. If you're new, start at 0.25% until 50 journaled trades follow the rules.
questions.lesson_line: The grade sets the risk. The stop turns it into shares.

wrong.0.25% to 0.5% of the account: That's the B- or lower size. A+ gets sized up.
wrong.Whatever fits the stop: The stop sets the shares, not the risk. The grade sets the risk.
wrong.2% to 3% of the account: Past every grade. A+ tops out at 1.5%.

questions.simple: 1% to 1.5%, because A+ is our cleanest grade and Green means full risk for it.

deeper.trap: Whatever fits the stop is the trap. The stop sets the shares, not the risk. Pick the risk from the grade first. Then shares = account × risk % ÷ (entry − stop), rounded down, then capped. A new trader starts at 0.25% until 50 journaled trades follow the rules.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook, E49, F65 and C37 (+2)

questions.q: When price reclaims the AVWAP from a high, the average holder since that high is back to even.
questions.why: True. Shannon: when they move back into a winning position, buyers are in control. Name the anchor; a line from a low tells another story.
questions.lesson_line: Every AVWAP tells one group's story. Say which group.

questions.q: It's the reclaim day. Write tomorrow's plan: how do you get in, and where's the stop?
questions.story: Above a rising 200-day, it closed back over its AVWAP after weeks under a flat line. Today's high is 17.68 and the low is 17.53.
choices: At the close, stop at the AVWAP
questions.why: Buy at market as it trades through 17.68, today's high, with the stop a few cents under the 17.53 low. NOW did exactly that the next morning: in at 17.70, stop 17.50. That's a 1.1% stop, nice and tight. Market orders put you in when it goes, not waiting on a fill that never comes. Write both down tonight and set the alert. The size follows from the stop.
questions.lesson_line: Entry and stop first. Write them down before the open.

wrong.Market through 17.68, stop at 17.53: A few cents under the low, not right on it. A tag of the exact low shouldn't take you out.
wrong.At the close, stop at the AVWAP: We buy as it trades through the trigger, never at the close. And the line isn't the stop.
wrong.Limit at 17.60, stop under 17.53: We use market orders through the trigger. A limit down there buys before it's proven, or never fills.

questions.simple: Buy at market as it trades through today's high, with the stop a few cents under today's low.

deeper.trap: The near-miss is a stop right on the low. Ours goes a few cents under it. The other trap is a limit under the trigger, which may never fill.

reasons: rests on held decisions D-003 (trigger) and D-008 (stop)
fixed before (cold check)

questions.q: How many of the seven do you buy this week?
questions.story: A correction just ended and our market filter turned Green. Seven leaders on your list are reclaiming their AVWAPs from their highs.
choices: A few, add more as they work
All seven, Green is full risk
None, wait a month after the turn
questions.answer: A few, add more as they work
questions.why: A few, and add more as they work. The first Green turn after a correction can be a head fake. Buy all seven, it fails, and seven stops hit at once. Half size on all seven is still seven positions failing together. Start with a few of the best. If they work, the market's telling you the turn is real, and you add names. Let the market earn your exposure.
questions.lesson_line: Green after a correction: a few first. Let the winners earn the next ones.

wrong.All seven, Green is full risk: Green is full risk per grade. After a correction we still start with a few.
wrong.None, wait a month after the turn: No rule makes you wait. Start with a few once it turns Green.
wrong.All seven at half size: Seven at half size is still seven positions. Start with a few.

questions.simple: A few. The first Green after a correction can fail, so let the first ones work first.

deeper.trap: The trap is the half-size answer. Seven positions at half size is still seven positions that can fail together. Start with a few and add more only as they work. Many leaders reclaiming at once is a good sign for the market, not an order to buy them all.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook, F68 (+2)

questions.q: Does that October undercut keep you out?
questions.story: The reclaim day. During the fall, the October low undercut the 200-day. Today it closes over the AVWAP and above the 200-day.
choices: No, it's today's close that counts
Yes, it can never touch the 200-day
questions.answer: No, it's today's close that counts
questions.why: No. We read the 200-day on the close the day you'd buy. Today's close is above it, so you're clear. An undercut weeks ago, in the middle of the fall, is history. It can feel like a broken stock, but a hard fall can drag a good stock under its 200-day for a bit. What matters is where it closes on the reclaim day.
questions.lesson_line: Read the 200-day on the close the day you buy.

wrong.Yes, it traded under the 200-day: The test is the close on the reclaim day, not every low before it.
wrong.Yes, it can never touch the 200-day: Touching it during the fall is history. Today's close decides.
wrong.No, a rising 200-day overrides it: Right call, wrong reason. A rising 200-day is a plus. The test is today's close above it.

questions.simple: No. We check the close on the reclaim day, and today's close is above the 200-day.

deeper.trap: The trap is reading the line as a history test. During the fall the low undercut the 200-day, and that feels like a broken stock. We read one thing: the close on the reclaim day against the 200-day. Above it, you're clear. A rising 200-day is then the better version.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook, B26, as the card reads it (+2)

questions.q: What do you tell yourself about the volume?
questions.story: Two reclaims trigger the same day. One came on 2.5x volume, the other on 0.6x. Both pass every gate on the card.

questions.answer: Volume did not sort winners here
questions.why: Volume did not sort winners here. In our scan the loudest reclaim days reached 3R less often than the quiet ones; the stop and the market did more.
questions.lesson_line: A loud reclaim day feels like proof. In our data it was not.

wrong.Only take the 2.5x one: Our scan found loud volume did not help. It is not a reason to drop the other.
wrong.Only take the 0.6x one: Quiet days did a little better, but no rule makes quiet a gate.

questions.q: Two days in, it's trading 49.30, just over your stop. The 50-day sits at 48.80. What do you do with the stop?
questions.story: You bought a reclaim at 50.00 with the stop at 49.00.
choices: Widen it by half an ATR
questions.why: Leave it. Your stop is your exit, and it only moves up. Never down, never wider. The 50-day sitting just under it is exactly the excuse that turns a small loss into a big one. If the stop hits, you take the loss you planned and look for the next trigger. The one time a stop goes lower is a gap through it, and this isn't one.
questions.lesson_line: The stop goes in once. After that it only climbs.

wrong.Lower it under the 50-day: That's moving the stop down. It only moves up.
wrong.Widen it by half an ATR: The stop never moves down or wider. The gap rule's the only exception, and this isn't a gap.
wrong.Cancel it, watch the close: Without the stop there's no exit. That's how you end up holding and hoping.

questions.simple: Leave it. The stop is your exit and it only ever moves up.
